stories.head: Fuel tanker fire on Cairo ring road kills 31
stories.say: A fuel tanker fire on a Cairo ring road has killed thirty-one people. Prosecutors say a speeding car clipped the tanker, which overturned and burst into flames.
stories.stand: Egypt's prosecutors say a car hit the tanker at speed on Wednesday, and the driver has been arrested.
body: A fire on the Ring Road around Cairo killed 31 people and injured 21 on Wednesday, Egypt's Public Prosecution said. The crash happened in the Waraq area of Giza, part of Greater Cairo.
According to the prosecutor's statement, a car struck the back of a fuel tanker while overtaking. The tanker overturned and hit a concrete barrier, and leaking fuel caught fire.
The driver has been arrested and reportedly admitted driving at about 70mph, prosecutors said. At least 27 vehicles were destroyed. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi offered condolences.

stories.head: Explosion and fire at Bangkok oil refinery injure at least 7
stories.say: An explosion at the Bangchak oil refinery in eastern Bangkok on Thursday sent black smoke over the city. At least seven people were hurt, four of them critically.
stories.stand: The fire at the Bangchak site was put out within an hour, city authorities said; the cause is being investigated.
body: An explosion and fire hit the Bangchak oil refinery and storage site in eastern Bangkok at around 3pm on Thursday, sending thick black smoke over the Thai capital.
At least seven people were injured, four of them critically, according to the Erawan Medical Center. Residents nearby were told to leave the area.

The Bangkok city authority said the fire was out less than an hour later. Bangchak Corporation confirmed the fire and said the cause was under investigation. The refinery is Thailand's only one in an urban area.

stories.head: Rescuers search flooded illegal gold mine in West Java
stories.say: Rescuers in West Java are pumping water from a flooded illegal gold mine, where officials say heavy rain sent a river into the shafts on Monday night.
stories.stand: Bodies have been recovered and more miners are believed trapped in the shafts in Bogor, south of Jakarta.
body: Rescuers in Indonesia are searching a flooded illegal gold mine in Bogor, West Java, after a nearby river burst its banks in heavy rain late on Monday.
Bodies have been recovered and more miners are believed to be trapped. The shaft is estimated at about 100 metres deep. Police said 11 miners got out before it flooded.

Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta search and rescue office, is leading the operation. Officials said nobody reported the flooding at first because the mine was illegal. State miner Antam said the site was not part of its operations.

stories.head: Eisenkot pushes to form Israel's next government
stories.say: Israel's opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot says coalition talks are moving at full speed. He has signed up Avigdor Liberman's party but is still short of a majority.
stories.stand: A month after the election, no bloc has 61 seats; Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government.
body: Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot says efforts to form a government are moving at full speed. President Isaac Herzog gave him the mandate after the 27 October election left no bloc with 61 seats.
On Tuesday his Yashar party agreed a coalition pact with Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu. Yair Golan's Democrats then said they were halting talks with Yashar.
Eisenkot's deadline is 6 December, which Herzog could extend. Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister. Whether Arab-led parties take part is the main sticking point.

stories.head: Judges urge prosecutors to rethink Netanyahu bribery charge
stories.say: Judges in Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial have urged prosecutors to consider dropping the only bribery charge. Netanyahu denies all wrongdoing.
stories.stand: The Jerusalem court said its comments were not an acquittal; the attorney general will review them.
body: Judges at the Jerusalem District Court have urged prosecutors to consider dropping the bribery allegation in Case 4000, the most serious charge against Benjamin Netanyahu.
The judges also questioned whether conduct in Case 2000 was a crime, and suggested an agreement in Case 1000, which concerns gifts from wealthy businessmen.

The court said its comments were not an acquittal and no charges have been dismissed. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said prosecutors would review them. Netanyahu denies wrongdoing; his trial began in May 2020.

stories.head: Two Italian technicians killed by drone debris in Kuwait
stories.say: Two Italian technicians have died in Kuwait after debris fell from drones being shot down. Kuwait blames Iran; Iran's military denies any attack.
stories.stand: Kuwait says it intercepted Iranian drones aimed at a vital site on Thursday; Iran denies carrying out the attack.
body: Two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia died after being hit by falling debris in Kuwait on Thursday, Italy's foreign ministry said. Kuwait said the debris came from Iranian drones it was intercepting.
Kuwait's defence ministry said the drones targeted a vital facility and that two other workers were wounded. Italy described the site as an air defence surveillance station.
Flights on the Europe to Gulf corridor were rerouted during the attack. Iran's military spokesperson denied any offensive operations and blamed Israel and the US.

stories.head: Kim Jong Un tours nuclear plants and calls for more weapons
stories.say: North Korea's Kim Jong Un has toured two nuclear material plants and called for battlefield nuclear weapons, state media say, after ignoring Donald Trump's offer of talks.
stories.stand: State media say Kim visited a new and an expanding plant on Wednesday; their locations were not disclosed.
body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited two nuclear material production plants on Wednesday, one newly opened and one being expanded, state news agency KCNA reported. Their locations were not given.
Kim called the country's nuclear status irreversible and urged the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons, KCNA said.
Donald Trump's offer of a meeting has gone unanswered. South Korea's defence ministry said it takes the remarks seriously.

stories.head: Guinea-Bissau delays elections by two years
stories.say: Guinea-Bissau's military-led government has pushed back presidential and parliamentary elections from next month to November twenty twenty-eight.
stories.stand: A decree from the transitional president cites a lack of technical, material and financial conditions.
body: Guinea-Bissau's transitional president, Major-General Horta Inta-a, issued a decree on Thursday delaying presidential and legislative elections from 6 December to November 2028.
The decree cites insufficient technical, material and financial conditions for the vote. The army seized power last November, overthrowing Umaro Sissoco Embalo.
The regional bloc ECOWAS had called for a short and transparent transition.

stories.say: Zambian police have banned a protest against a push to remove presidential term limits, which could let Hakainde Hichilema seek a third term.
stories.stand: Police cited the risk of clashes after a pro-government youth group announced a rival march.

Police cited the risk of clashes after a pro-government youth group announced a rival demonstration.

stories.head: Ukraine defends drone strike on Russian ships in Libya
stories.say: Ukraine says its drone strike on Russian ships at Benghazi was legitimate self-defence. Libya's eastern army says two of its personnel died and has vowed a response.
stories.stand: The attack sank one Russian ship and damaged another at the Benghazi naval base on Sunday.
body: Drone attacks on Sunday sank a Russian ship and damaged another at the naval base in Benghazi, eastern Libya. Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the targets were a corvette and a cargo ship carrying military equipment.
The Libyan National Army, which controls the east and has ties to Russia, confirmed that two of its personnel died, and vowed a response.
Sybiha called the strike legitimate self-defence. The UN mission in Libya warned against making the country a battleground for foreign conflicts.

stories.head: Leaked data suggests at least 490,000 Russian soldiers killed
stories.say: Leaked Russian government records, analysed by the BBC, suggest at least four hundred and ninety thousand Russian soldiers have died in the war in Ukraine.
stories.stand: The Kremlin says only its defence ministry can release casualty figures.
body: Leaked Russian government data analysed by BBC News suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since February 2022, CBS News reported.
The dataset was obtained by pro-Ukraine hacking groups and includes more than 11 million death records. The independent Russian outlet Mediazona estimates the true toll is likely around 700,000.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said only Russia's defence ministry can disclose casualty figures.

stories.say: Ukraine says it has used a laser for the first time to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone, though an adviser says mass production is still some way off.
stories.stand: A presidential adviser credited the Blysk laser system, made by a private Ukrainian firm.

stories.head: Germany arrests two Iraqis over alleged synagogue plot
stories.say: German police have arrested two Iraqi men suspected of belonging to an Iran-linked group that investigators say planned to target synagogues.
stories.stand: Prosecutors say the men belong to a group the US calls a front for Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
body: German authorities arrested two Iraqi men in Cologne and Heidelberg on suspicion of membership of a terrorist organisation, federal prosecutors said.

Investigators allege the group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, planned to target synagogues in Cologne and another European city. The US says the group is a front for Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps.
More than 250 officers searched 17 locations in three German states. The investigation is ongoing.

stories.head: Serbia's new ruling party proposes reality TV curbs and 4-day week
stories.say: Serbia's new Student List party wants to limit reality TV to forty-five minutes a day after eleven at night, and let employers offer a four-day week.
stories.stand: The proposals, published on the party's website, follow its election win over Aleksandar Vucic.
body: Serbia's Student List party, which ousted longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in an October election, has proposed capping reality TV on terrestrial channels at 45 minutes a day, shown only after 11pm.
Live reality broadcasts on those channels would be banned. Paid channels would be exempt.
The party also proposes that employers could opt into a four-day week of 32 hours with unchanged pay. The plans are proposals, not law.

stories.say: Australia and Solomon Islands have signed a treaty under which Honiara pledges not to host any foreign military base, a move seen as a blow to China.
stories.stand: Solomon Islands must consult Australia on national security under the deal, signed in Canberra.
body: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale signed a treaty in Canberra on Wednesday.
Solomon Islands pledged not to allow its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base, and to consult Australia on national security and sensitive infrastructure.
The ABC reported that the 2022 security pact with China will be allowed to lapse in April 2027. Wale declined to confirm that, citing a non-disclosure clause.

stories.head: £8bn deal aims to get nuclear submarines back to sea faster
stories.say: The government has handed Babcock an eight billion pound contract to speed up maintenance of the Royal Navy's nuclear submarines, with dry docks running around the clock.
stories.stand: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says the deal will create about 3,000 skilled jobs, mainly in Plymouth, Glasgow and Bristol.
body: The Ministry of Defence has awarded Babcock a five-year contract worth around £8bn to cut maintenance time for the Royal Navy's submarines. Dry dock yards will run around the clock, ITV News reported.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting announced the deal at HMNB Devonport in Plymouth on Thursday, calling it the biggest procurement decision of this Parliament.
The MoD expects about 3,000 skilled jobs. At HMNB Clyde, Faslane, 900 jobs and 450 apprentice and graduate places are planned. Babcock says it is the largest contract in its history.

stories.head: Stalking to become a standalone offence with 10-year maximum
stories.say: Stalking is to become a standalone offence in England and Wales, with a maximum of ten years in prison, and victims will no longer have to show they felt fear.
stories.stand: A review found the current law 'cluttered and confused'; the changes will come when parliamentary time allows.
body: Stalking is to be made a standalone offence in England and Wales, the Home Office said, after a review led by barrister Richard Wright KC found the current law cluttered and confused.
Stalkers could face up to 10 years in prison, and victims would no longer need to show they suffered fear or distress. The changes will be legislated when parliamentary time allows.
An estimated 1.9 million people experienced stalking in the year to March, up from 1.4 million a year earlier, according to the Crime Survey for England and Wales.

stories.head: Tube drivers' strike disrupts London into Friday morning
stories.say: An R M T strike by London Underground drivers over a four-day week plan has shut the Circle and Piccadilly lines, with disruption until around midday on Friday.
stories.stand: It is the first of a series of 24-hour walkouts; Aslef members backed TfL's revised offer and are working.
body: RMT members among London Underground drivers began a 24-hour strike at noon on Thursday in a dispute over a four-day week.
No Circle or Piccadilly line trains ran on Thursday. Services start later than usual on Friday, with disruption until around midday and a return to normal by around 6pm.
Transport for London revised its voluntary four-day week offer, and the Aslef union backed it. Further RMT strikes are planned for December, January and February.

stories.say: Forecasters say freezing rain could coat roads and paths in clear glaze ice on Thursday night and Friday, mainly on higher ground in northern Britain.
stories.stand: Scotland, northern England and north Wales are most at risk, the Met Office says.
body: The Met Office has forecast freezing rain from Thursday night into Friday, mainly over higher ground in northern Britain, ITV News reported.
Freezing rain falls as liquid and freezes on contact with surfaces below zero, forming a clear coating known as glaze ice that is hard to see.
Scotland, parts of northern England and north Wales are most at risk. Drivers, pedestrians and cyclists are warned of slippery surfaces, and ice could build up on trees and power lines.

stories.stand: The family were not at home; the court heard cufflinks and a clock were taken.
body: Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, both Albanian nationals, appeared at Norwich Magistrates' Court on Wednesday charged over a break-in at Anmer Hall on the Sandringham estate in Norfolk.

Prince William, Kate and their children were not at the house. Neither man was asked to plead, and both were remanded in custody.

stories.head: Average private rent in England rises to £269 a week
stories.say: Private renters in England now pay an average of two hundred and sixty-nine pounds a week, official survey figures show, and in London it is four hundred and thirty-nine.
stories.stand: The English Housing Survey finds private renting still makes up about a fifth of households.
body: Average weekly private rent in England rose from £250 to £269, according to the English Housing Survey for 2025-26, Mortgage Solutions reported.
In London the average rose from £393 to £439 a week. Elsewhere in England it rose from £207 to £219.
The private rented sector had 4.8 million households, or 19% of the total. Private renters spent an average of 34% of household income on housing costs.

stories.say: The Metropolitan Police has accepted all ten recommendations of an independent review of its reforms, which says trust among Black and gay Londoners still lags behind.
stories.stand: The review assessed progress since the 2023 Casey Review of the force.
body: The Metropolitan Police has accepted all ten recommendations of the Fairfield Review, an independent assessment of reform since the 2023 Casey Review.

stories.say: A family court magistrate has been formally advised for misconduct after remarks about migrants in Crewe that colleagues found inappropriate.
stories.stand: The judicial watchdog found Neil Stevenson breached guidance on impartiality and respect.
body: Neil Stevenson, a magistrate in the Family Court at Liverpool, has been disciplined for comments about migrants and immigration in Crewe town centre, the Judicial Conduct Investigations Office said.
The remarks were made to colleagues in a retiring room between cases. Colleagues found them racially insensitive or at least highly inappropriate, the office said.
The Lord Chancellor and a senior judge issued him formal advice. Stevenson apologised and said he had not meant the comments to be racist.

stories.head: Tagging before release to expand to 83 prisons by March
stories.say: More prisoners will be fitted with electronic tags before they leave jail, with the scheme growing to eighty-three prisons by the end of March, the Ministry of Justice says.
stories.stand: The 'tagging at source' scheme is part of a £100m investment in electronic monitoring.
body: The Ministry of Justice says it will expand fitting electronic tags to offenders before they leave prison, a scheme it calls tagging at source.
Six pilot prisons began in October 2025. The scheme will reach 16 prisons in December, 50 in January and 83 by the end of March.
A three-month pilot at Croydon and Highbury Corner magistrates' courts is also fitting tags. The expansion is part of a £100m investment in tagging.

stories.head: UK net migration falls to 77,000, lowest since 1997 outside Covid
stories.say: UK net migration fell to an estimated seventy-seven thousand in the year to June, the Office for National Statistics says, down from two hundred and four thousand a year earlier.
stories.stand: The ONS links the fall to fewer people arriving from outside the EU to work or study.
body: Net migration to the UK fell to an estimated 77,000 in the year to June 2026, down from 204,000 in the previous 12 months, the Office for National Statistics said on Thursday.
It is the lowest annual figure since 1997, leaving aside the Covid period. An estimated 738,000 people arrived and 661,000 left.
The ONS linked the fall to fewer non-EU citizens coming to work or study. More British nationals left than arrived. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the government had restored control.

stories.head: Burnham brings in bill to end most post-Brexit food checks
stories.say: The government is introducing a bill to put its new food and drink deal with the EU into law, ending most post-Brexit checks and linking Britain to the EU carbon market.
stories.stand: The Conservatives say the savings on weekly shopping will be a few pennies.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is formally introducing a Cutting Costs Bill to Parliament on Thursday, ITV News reported.

The bill would implement a sanitary and phytosanitary deal agreed at last week's UK-EU summit, ending most post-Brexit food and drink checks. It would also link the UK to the EU emissions trading system.
Ministers expect businesses to pass savings on to shoppers. Conservative shadow Treasury minister Richard Fuller said the savings would amount to a few pennies on weekly shopping.

stories.say: The government is due to publish more papers on the vetting of Peter Mandelson before he became ambassador in Washington, after police dropped their objection.
stories.stand: Security minister Dan Jarvis was due to make a Commons statement on Thursday.
body: The government is expected to publish more papers about the vetting of Lord Peter Mandelson before he was sent to Washington as US ambassador, ITV News reported.
Security minister Dan Jarvis was due to make a Commons statement on Thursday. The Metropolitan Police had asked for some documents to be withheld but now says they can be released.

Mandelson was sacked last year after details of his links to Jeffrey Epstein emerged. He was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office; he has not been charged and denies the allegations.

stories.stand: Timms says Pip should stay a cash-first benefit as claimant numbers reach a record.
body: A review of Personal Independence Payment led by work and pensions minister Sir Stephen Timms will recommend changes to rehumanise the system, ITV News reported.
Timms says Pip should remain a cash-first benefit, with a fast track for people with the most severe conditions and those receiving end-of-life care.
Entitled claimants in England and Wales have reached a record 4.09 million. Spending rose from £16.3bn in 2019-20 to £27.3bn in 2024-25. A welfare white paper is expected early next year.

stories.say: Donald Trump has called official growth figures released before the midterms fake, after they were revised up. He gave no evidence; statisticians say revisions follow a fixed timetable.
stories.stand: Third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3% from an advance estimate of 3.4%.
body: President Donald Trump accused the Commerce Department of deliberately issuing wrong growth figures before the midterm elections, and demanded an investigation. He provided no evidence.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday revised third-quarter annualised growth up to 4.3%, from an advance estimate of 3.4% published on 29 October.
The bureau says routine revisions follow a set timetable regardless of the political calendar. Trump's Republicans suffered heavy losses in the 3 November elections.

stories.head: Judge refuses long-term ban on taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads
stories.say: A US federal judge has declined to extend a ban on government-made ads that Democrats say promote Donald Trump, though she said their legal claim is likely to succeed.
stories.stand: The Democratic National Committee sued over at least 11 ads paid for partly by a Homeland Security contract.
body: US District Judge Loren AliKhan declined on Wednesday to extend a temporary order against government-made ads that the Democratic National Committee says promote President Donald Trump.

The DNC challenged at least 11 ads paid for at least partly by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. The judge wrote that the DNC was likely to succeed on its claim that using public money for them broke the law.
The Justice Department said public funds were no longer being used to air the ads. The White House has called them public service announcements.

stories.head: EU budget summit ends without a deal
stories.say: EU leaders have left a Brussels summit without agreeing the bloc's next seven-year budget, with Emmanuel Macron setting the thirty-first of December as the absolute limit.
stories.stand: Leaders split over António Costa's €1.78 trillion proposal, and Friday's talks were cancelled.
body: EU leaders ended a summit in Brussels on Thursday without agreeing the bloc's next seven-year budget, Euronews reported. Friday's talks were cancelled.
European Council President António Costa proposed a €1.78 trillion package, but it drew pushback from countries wanting deeper cuts and from those resisting them.
French President Emmanuel Macron said 31 December was the absolute limit for a deal. A new loan for Ukraine was also under discussion. Any budget needs the backing of all 27 member states.

stories.stand: About 40 figures have declared or are seen as possible candidates, five months before the vote.
body: Around 40 people have declared or are seen as potential candidates in France's presidential election, about five months away, Euronews reported.
Candidates need at least 500 endorsements from elected officials, and mayors are the largest pool. The annual mayors' congress has become a campaign venue.
David Lisnard, mayor of Cannes and leader of the Nouvelle Énergie party, was re-elected head of the Association of Mayors of France on Wednesday. Polls suggest Marine Le Pen's National Rally leads.

body: Andalusia, once a Socialist stronghold, has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People's Party and the far-right Vox since May's regional election, Al Jazeera reported.
National opinion polls place the PP first, the PSOE second and Vox third, with the two right-wing parties expected to have enough seats to govern together.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo reportedly prefers a minority government backed by Vox. Vox wants to repeal Spain's 2004 gender-based violence law.

stories.say: The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs of up to thirty-five per cent on goods from China, the EU and twelve other economies, over what it calls excess factory capacity.
stories.stand: Some Chinese goods would face a total rate of 45%; a hearing is set for 25 January.
body: The US Trade Representative has proposed new tariffs on imports from 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan, India and Vietnam, after a probe into what it calls excess industrial capacity.
Proposed duties range from 15% to 35%, ITV News reported. Some Chinese goods would face a new 20% tariff, taking their total to 45%. Brazil faces a 10% tariff on aircraft, which would hit Embraer.
Semiconductors from Taiwan and South Korea would be exempt, and Australia is excluded. A hearing is set for 25 January, so the duties are likely to start in February or March.

stories.say: Poundland has gone into administration after its owners failed to find a buyer, putting around eleven thousand jobs at risk weeks before Christmas.
stories.stand: The chain's roughly 600 stores will keep trading while administrators AlixPartners seek a sale.
body: Poundland entered administration on Wednesday after its owners failed to find a buyer before a deadline, ITV News reported. Around 11,000 jobs are at risk.
The discount chain runs roughly 600 stores, which will keep trading while administrators AlixPartners look for a sale. The group is likely to be broken up.
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland for £1 early last year and later closed more than 100 shops. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the news deeply concerning.

stories.stand: The regulator blames a jump in gas prices linked to conflict in the Middle East.
body: Ofgem's price cap will rise by 26% from January, adding £443 a year to take a typical household bill in England, Scotland and Wales to £2,166, ITV News reported.
The regulator linked the rise to a jump in gas prices in October tied to conflict in the Middle East. About 10 million households on fixed tariffs are unaffected.
About 20 million households will get a £100 payment from January. Analysts at Cornwall Insight forecast a 1% fall from April 2027.

stories.head: Argentina's economy shrinks for a second quarter in a row
stories.say: Argentina has entered a technical recession, with official data showing the economy shrank one point eight per cent from July to September.
stories.stand: Weak consumption is weighing on President Javier Milei's economic record, official data show.
body: Argentina's economy shrank 1.8% from July to September, following a 1% fall in the previous quarter, according to the statistics agency Indec's monthly activity indicator, Euronews reported.
Two quarters of contraction meet the common definition of a technical recession. The government urges caution, and final GDP figures are due on 16 December.
Unemployment reached 7.9% in the second quarter, the highest since Milei took office.

stories.stand: National consumer authorities will monitor its compliance across the EU.
body: The European Commission said Temu has committed to changes to bring it in line with EU consumer protection rules, Euronews reported.
The commitments include clearer pricing, simpler returns and refunds, more reliable reviews and the removal of forced gamification features.

body: A majority of eurozone countries backed Pablo Hernández de Cos, 55, to succeed Christine Lagarde at the European Central Bank, after a summit in Brussels on Thursday, Euronews reported.

stories.head: Hera probe shows crater left by NASA's asteroid impact
stories.say: Europe's Hera spacecraft has sent back its first close-up images of Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA deliberately struck in twenty twenty-two, showing a huge crater and drifting boulders.
stories.stand: The asteroid survived the DART impact, but its rotation is now chaotic, mission scientists say.
body: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has returned its first close-up images of Dimorphos, the 151-metre asteroid that NASA's DART probe hit in 2022, Euronews reported.
The images, at 2.7 metres per pixel, show a crater described as the size of a sports stadium, and hundreds of boulders drifting around the system. The asteroid was not destroyed.
The 2022 impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit around its larger companion, Didymos, by about 33 minutes. Project manager Ian Carnelli called the scene complete chaos.

body: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has become the first Pakistani to enter orbit and the first foreign astronaut to visit China's Tiangong space station, ITV News reported.
He flew on the Shenzhou-24 mission from the Jiuquan launch centre. The capsule docked about three hours after launch. He is due back next week.

stories.say: Senegal's football federation has called Moroccan claims of contact with a sports court arbitrator absolutely false, after the court ruled Senegal the rightful Afcon champions.
stories.stand: The Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned CAF's decision to award Morocco the 2025 title.
body: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Senegal are the rightful 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners, overturning CAF's decision to award the title to Morocco, Al Jazeera reported.
Senegal won the January final 1-0 after extra time, but CAF later awarded Morocco a 3-0 win after Senegal's players walked off over a penalty.
Morocco's federation alleged contact between Senegal's federation president, Abdoulaye Fall, and a CAS arbitrator. Fall called the claim absolutely false.

stories.head: Besiktas fans clash with Georgian police over Palestinian flag
stories.say: A Europa League match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia was halted for about thirty minutes after fans clashed with police over a Palestinian flag.
stories.stand: Besiktas went on to win 2-1 in Batumi.
body: Besiktas fans clashed with Georgian police after unfurling a Palestinian flag during a Europa League match against Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Batumi, Al Jazeera reported.
The game was suspended for about 30 minutes at 0-0. Besiktas won 2-1 when play resumed.
Besiktas called the security forces' response disproportionate. UEFA had moved the game to Georgia.

stories.say: Bayern Munich say Jamal Musiala was first examined for absence-like neurological symptoms in April twenty twenty-five, more than sixteen months before his condition was announced.
stories.stand: The club held talks with his management on Tuesday amid contract speculation.
body: Bayern Munich say midfielder Jamal Musiala was first examined on 22 April 2025 for absence-like symptoms, Al Jazeera reported. His condition was announced in August.
Musiala has said he has temporary, brief and easily treatable absences caused by a neurological dysfunction.
Bayern held talks with his management on Tuesday. He is under contract until 2030.

stories.head: Qatar Grand Prix weekend begins with Antonelli already champion
stories.say: Practice for the Qatar Grand Prix begins on Friday, with Kimi Antonelli already crowned world champion and Max Verstappen chasing a fourth straight win at Lusail.
stories.stand: Pirelli's hardest tyres and a 27-lap limit per set make a two-stop race effectively mandatory.
body: The Qatar Grand Prix weekend at Lusail starts with practice on Friday, with the race on Sunday, Formula 1 said. Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli has already clinched the drivers' title.
Max Verstappen is second in the standings after winning in Las Vegas, and has won the last three Qatar Grands Prix.

Pirelli has limited each set of tyres to 27 laps, making a two-stop race effectively mandatory. Verstappen will work with engineer Tom Hart, as Gianpiero Lambiase misses the race, RacingNews365 reported.

stories.head: Fossil 'Lizzie' was a gilled water animal, not an early reptile
stories.say: X-ray scans show a three hundred and forty-five million year old Scottish fossil called Lizzie had internal gills, so it was probably not an early reptile as long thought.
stories.stand: Synchrotron scans revealed gills and fish-like teeth in Westlothiana lizziae, found in 1984.
body: Westlothiana lizziae, a 345-million-year-old fossil found in Scotland in 1984 and nicknamed Lizzie, was long considered an early member of the reptile line, ScienceDaily reported.
X-ray scans at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility revealed internal gills and fish-like teeth, suggesting it was aquatic or amphibious. The study is published in Nature.
The researchers, from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford among others, say some footprints credited to early reptiles may come from animals like it.

stories.head: Russian cargo ship docks at space station on Thanksgiving
stories.say: Russia's Progress ninety-seven cargo craft docked with the International Space Station on Thursday morning, delivering about three tons of food, fuel and supplies.
stories.stand: It will stay about eight months before a planned destructive re-entry carrying rubbish.
body: The Roscosmos Progress 97 cargo spacecraft docked with the International Space Station at 7:08am Eastern time on Thursday, NASA said. It attached to the Earth-facing port of the Rassvet module.
It launched on 24 November on a Soyuz rocket from Baikonur in Kazakhstan, carrying about three tons of food, fuel and supplies for the Expedition 75 crew.
The craft will stay about eight months before leaving for a planned destructive re-entry that disposes of rubbish.

stories.head: Europa Clipper to swing past Earth on 3 December
stories.say: NASA's Europa Clipper will fly past Earth on the third of December, using its gravity for a boost towards Jupiter, where it should arrive in twenty thirty.
stories.stand: The flyby will also test all nine of its instruments, NASA says.
body: NASA's Europa Clipper will fly past Earth on Thursday 3 December, with its closest approach west of Africa at about 3,140 to 3,450 km, NASA said.
Earth's gravity will give the 6,000kg spacecraft a boost towards Jupiter. All nine instruments will collect data as a calibration exercise.
The probe is due to begin orbiting Jupiter in April 2030 to study whether the ocean under Europa's ice could support life.

stories.head: Deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf show genetic warning signs
stories.say: All five deep-sea species studied in the Gulf show genetic signs linked to extinction risk, and one lanternfish lost about eight per cent of its genetic diversity in twelve years.
stories.stand: Florida International University researchers analysed 12 years of genetic data from 486 specimens.
body: Researchers at Florida International University analysed 12 years of genetic data from 486 specimens of three lanternfish and two deep-sea shrimp species in the Gulf, ScienceDaily reported. The study is in Nature Communications.
All five species showed genetic traits linked to extinction risk. One lanternfish, Diaphus dumerilii, lost about 8% of its genetic diversity in 12 years.
The signals indicate risk rather than documented extinctions. The study found no direct link to the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill.

stories.head: Most brain cells respond to many kinds of information, mouse study finds
stories.say: A study of mouse brains across forty-three regions found most neurons respond to many kinds of information, with specialised cells the exception rather than the rule.
stories.stand: Researchers from Columbia, EPFL and the Paris Brain Institute published the work in Nature.
body: Researchers analysed recordings from 43 regions of the mouse cortex and found most neurons respond to many kinds of information, ScienceDaily reported. The study is published in Nature.
Specialised neurons exist but are the exceptions, said Stefano Fusi of Columbia University's Zuckerman Institute. Neurons in primary sensory areas were more specialised.
The team included researchers from EPFL in Lausanne and the Paris Brain Institute. The findings come from mice; comparisons with human neurons are still under way.

stories.head: Robot-assisted knee replacement no better after a year, big UK trial finds
stories.say: The largest trial of robot-assisted knee replacement found no real difference in recovery after a year, and the robot added about nine hundred and fifty pounds per operation.
stories.stand: The RACER-Knee trial at 10 UK hospitals is published in The Lancet; ten-year follow-up is planned.
body: The RACER-Knee trial compared robot-assisted knee replacement with conventional surgery in 339 patients at 10 UK hospitals, ScienceDaily reported. It is published in The Lancet.
At one year there was no meaningful difference in the main outcome, nor in walking, pain or the likelihood of further surgery. Serious complications did not increase.
Robotic surgery added about 10.5 minutes and roughly £950 per operation and was not cost-effective for the NHS in the first year. The trial was led by the University of Warwick.

stories.head: Kenyan court rules US-backed Ebola quarantine site unconstitutional
stories.say: Kenya's High Court has ruled the government broke the constitution by allowing a US-backed Ebola quarantine centre at a military base without public consultation.
stories.stand: Work on the 50-bed facility near Nanyuki must stop until the deal is disclosed and the public consulted.
body: Kenya's High Court ruled that the government breached the constitution by allowing construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine facility at Laikipia airbase near Nanyuki, Al Jazeera reported.
Judge Patricia Nyaundi said the government should have disclosed the details of the agreement with the US and sought public input. Further work on the 50-bed facility must stop until it does.
The site was meant to quarantine people exposed to Ebola, including US citizens. The government had not commented on the ruling.

stories.head: Trump held millions in Nvidia stock as he pressed for Huang's return
stories.say: Financial disclosures show Donald Trump held between thirteen and fifty-eight million dollars in Nvidia stock while he pushed for Jensen Huang's return as chief executive.
stories.stand: The White House says third-party managers make all investment decisions for the president's portfolio.
body: Donald Trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to financial disclosures reported by CBS News.
Nvidia shares rose more than 30% when Jensen Huang returned as chief executive on Monday. Trump said he had convinced the company to rehire him.
The White House said third-party managers make all investment decisions and that the portfolio mirrors broad indexes. Ethics experts quoted by CBS called it a conflict of interest.

stories.head: UK suspends tariffs on more than 100 food and other products
stories.say: The Treasury has suspended tariffs on more than a hundred products, including baked beans and chocolate, saying shoppers could save up to a hundred and eighty-five million pounds a year.
stories.stand: The suspensions last until December 2028, or December 2027 for fertilisers.
body: The Treasury suspended tariffs on more than 100 products from Thursday, including baked beans, garlic, chocolate, marmalade and plant-based drinks, GOV.UK said.
It estimates consumer savings of up to £185 million a year, with lower-income households benefiting most. With a package announced in June, savings could reach up to £595 million a year.
The suspensions run until December 2028, and until December 2027 for fertilisers. Chancellor John Healey said the government would help where it could.
